content:
Fireflies.ai Meeting Transcript

Title: Helio Health x Redwood - POC check-in (version pinning + rollbacks)
Date: 2025-03-05
Time: 10:02 AM - 10:49 AM PT
Duration: 47 minutes
Meeting ID: ff-20250305-helio-poc-checkin-7b9f2c1a

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Avery Johnson, Bruno Silva, Rachel Kim
Helio Health: Priya Nair, Elena Ruiz, Mark Feldman, Tom Sato

Auto-summary (generated)
- Helio wants deterministic version pinning for Redwood Private so they can avoid incident-driven upgrades and keep change control predictable.
- Redwood walked through LTS channel expectations: slower-change, monthly patches, out-of-band security fixes, and clear backport criteria.
- Discussed rollback mechanics: pinning tags by patch version, keeping N-1 artifacts available, and using Helm/installer to flip back quickly.
- Security asked about artifact integrity: checksums, provenance, and SBOM availability for LTS builds.

Topics
- LTS channel vs mainline runtime cadence
- Version pinning (installer + Helm)
- Rollback procedure and operational churn
- Release notes expectations (known issues, upgrade notes, compatibility)
- Artifact verification (sha256, signing/provenance, SBOM)

Questions captured
- Can we pin to an exact patch (e.g., 1.18.1-lts) and prevent auto-upgrades?
- What does rollback look like under Helm when there’s a runtime crash or latency regression?
- How quickly do you ship an out-of-band security patch and how do we get notified?
- Do you provide SBOMs for the runtime container and do they map to a commit/tag?

Transcript

[00:00] Avery Johnson: Alright, I think we’re recording. Cool. Thanks everyone for making time. This is the weekly POC check-in. Today we said we’d focus on version pinning and rollbacks in Private, and also how the LTS channel reduces… like, operational churn. Priya, do you want to kick with what you all hit this week?

[00:18] Priya Nair: Yeah. So we got the Private stack up in our staging cluster. Basic inference is fine. The issue is more operational. Our change board is already asking, like, “Are you going to be forced onto new runtime versions every couple weeks?” Because we saw you released 1.18, then 1.18-dot-something, and we can’t do that. We need a stable baseline.

[00:40] Elena Ruiz: And for the POC we can move fast, but for prod it’s… we need the ability to pin, test, and then roll forward on our schedule.

[00:50] Avery Johnson: Yup. Makes sense. That’s exactly why we’ve been building the Runtime LTS channel. Bruno can go deep on the mechanics. Rachel can cover what “supportable” means for enterprise.

[01:02] Bruno Silva: Hey everyone. So, at a high level: for Private you’ll have two knobs—installer and Helm. Both can pin the runtime image tag to an exact version. For LTS it would look like “runtime: 1.18.1-lts” or whatever patch you’re on. The key is it’s not “latest” and it’s not a floating “lts” pointer unless you choose that.

[01:25] Tom Sato: Sorry, when you say “floating pointer,” like a channel tag that advances automatically?

[01:29] Bruno Silva: Exactly. Some customers want “lts” and it moves monthly. But for regulated workflows we typically recommend pinning to the exact patch and then you explicitly change it after validation.

[01:41] Mark Feldman: And it won’t auto-update under us? Like, no background fetch that changes a digest?

[01:47] Bruno Silva: Right. If you pin by tag, it depends on your registry behavior, but we publish immutable tags and also you can pin by digest. In the Private installer we support “image:tag” and “image@sha256:…”. We also publish checksums for the artifacts and a provenance file that maps to the git commit and build pipeline run.

[02:10] Priya Nair: Okay, pinning by digest is probably what security will want. But operationally, our platform team prefers semantic versions in the manifest.

[02:19] Bruno Silva: Totally. You can do both: keep the semantic version as the “desired” and validate it matches the digest from our release notes. Some customers store a little lockfile in their GitOps repo.

[02:30] Rachel Kim: And from a support perspective, if you’re on 1.18.1-lts, our on-call and support workflow will treat that as a supported baseline through the LTS window. You won’t be told “upgrade to latest mainline” as the first step.

[02:46] Elena Ruiz: That’s been a pain with… honestly with our current self-hosted vLLM setup. The answer is always “pull HEAD.”

[02:54] Avery Johnson: Yeah, exactly. LTS is meant to avoid that. We’ll talk about patch cadence too.

[03:02] Priya Nair: Before we go there, can we talk rollback? Like, worst case, we deploy an LTS patch and it regresses latency. What do we do? Is it just Helm rollback and you’re done?

[03:15] Bruno Silva: Practically yes. If you deploy via Helm and you keep your old values, you can “helm rollback” to the previous release revision. The runtime image would revert to the previous tag/digest. The gotcha is: you need to ensure the old image is still available in your registry, especially if you mirror artifacts internally.

[03:33] Tom Sato: We mirror. We have an internal Harbor registry. So we’d pull from you, then push internally.

[03:38] Bruno Silva: Great. Then rollback is deterministic. You just switch back to N-1. For the installer path, it’s similar: the installer keeps an “installed version” record and you can redeploy with the previous version pinned.

[03:54] Mark Feldman: Is there any data migration that would make rollback unsafe? Like, do you touch persistent state?

[04:01] Bruno Silva: For the serving runtime itself, we don’t do schema migrations as part of patch updates. Most state is in-memory: KV cache, scheduler queues, etc. If you’re using observability exports, that’s external. So rollback is typically safe. The one exception is if you change config defaults that alter behavior; but LTS is specifically freezing many of those to reduce surprises.

[04:23] Priya Nair: You said “freezing defaults.” Like kernel tuning and batching?

[04:28] Bruno Silva: Yep. On mainline we may introduce a new batching heuristic or kernel autotune change. On LTS we freeze experimental heuristics unless they’re explicitly opted-in. That’s part of the slower-change promise.

[04:41] Avery Johnson: The business framing: you get predictable monthly patch day, and you’re not forced into adopting new scheduling behavior just to get a critical fix.

[04:51] Elena Ruiz: Can you say what “monthly” means? Like first Tuesday? Or just “around once a month.”

[04:58] Rachel Kim: We’re standardizing it. The target is a monthly patch cadence, with out-of-band security fixes if needed. We can align on a window with you—some customers want “second week of the month.” But the important part is it’s not every week.

[05:13] Priya Nair: Okay. That helps. For us, change board wants like quarterly feature changes but security patches as needed.

[05:22] Mark Feldman: And security patches… what’s the SLA? If there’s a CVE, how fast do we get a patch on the LTS line?

[05:30] Avery Johnson: We can share the formal language, but directionally: for critical vulnerabilities we do an out-of-band patch and we’ll notify you via support channels, plus release notes with CVE references. Hanae on our side runs vuln response, but for this call we can keep it practical.

[05:49] Mark Feldman: Practical is good.

[05:51] Bruno Silva: Practically, you’d receive an “x.y.z-lts” patch with release notes calling out “Security” category. We also provide checksums and the provenance so you can verify what you mirrored internally.

[06:06] Tom Sato: What’s the comms path? Email? Slack?

[06:09] Rachel Kim: For pilot we can do both. For GA, we typically do email to your named admins + support ticket updates. Some customers also want a webhook into their internal change system. But at minimum: release notes URL, artifact URL, and a “mandatory vs optional” designation.

[06:28] Priya Nair: Mandatory vs optional is important. If you say “mandatory,” we can fast-track.

[06:33] Avery Johnson: Right. Criteria is usually Sev1 crash, active exploit, or something impacting reliability broadly.

[06:41] Elena Ruiz: On rollbacks, one more detail: do you support having two runtime deployments side-by-side? Like canary.

[06:48] Bruno Silva: Yes. In Kubernetes you can deploy a canary namespace or separate release name and route a small fraction of traffic. For the runtime specifically, you can do it at the service level or via your ingress. Redwood Console has rollout tooling for Hosted/Dedicated, but for Private you manage it via your cluster routing. We can share a basic canary playbook.

[07:10] Tom Sato: We do Argo Rollouts. So that’s fine.

[07:13] Bruno Silva: Perfect. Then you can canary 5%, watch latency and error rates, and then proceed.

[07:21] Avery Johnson: Maybe we should talk about what you saw last week—there was that latency spike on your long prompts?

[07:27] Elena Ruiz: Yeah. It’s not huge but we saw p95 creep when we changed a scheduler flag. We reverted and it went away. That’s why we’re nervous about “defaults changing” between releases.

[07:40] Bruno Silva: That’s precisely what LTS tries to avoid. On LTS, we aim for minimal diff and a strict perf gate. If a backport is accepted, it goes through perf canary benchmarks with thresholds. If it regresses, it doesn’t ship, or it requires an explicit waiver.

[07:58] Priya Nair: What are the thresholds? I know it’s not exact because GPUs are noisy.

[08:02] Bruno Silva: Yeah, benchmarks are noisy. But typically we gate p95 latency and throughput deltas. Like p95 can’t regress beyond a small percent on canonical workloads. I don’t want to quote a number wrong here, but we can share the doc. The point is: it’s not “best effort,” it’s a release gate.

[08:22] Tom Sato: Is this for all GPU types? We’re on L4 in staging, but prod is A100.

[08:27] Bruno Silva: We cover the common SKUs. For LTS we specifically include enterprise SKUs like A100/H100 and also L4 because people use it for cost. If your prod is A100, we’ll make sure your key workload is represented.

[08:43] Mark Feldman: Switching to compliance: you mentioned SBOM. Do you provide one for each runtime image?

[08:50] Bruno Silva: We’re adding SBOM generation for LTS artifacts. For the pilot, we can provide a stub or partial SBOM depending on where the build pipeline is at. For GA, the intention is each release has an SBOM reference in the release artifacts.

[09:08] Mark Feldman: “Stub” is not ideal for prod.

[09:10] Avery Johnson: Understood. For the POC we can proceed, but we’ll be transparent on what’s available. Rachel, can you speak to timeline?

[09:18] Rachel Kim: For the pilot phase, we can provide checksums and provenance reliably. SBOM will be in the GA checklist. We can set expectations in the pilot agreement so procurement isn’t surprised.

[09:32] Priya Nair: Okay. Another operational thing: if we pin to 1.18.1-lts, how long is that supported? Like you said 6 to 12 months.

[09:41] Avery Johnson: Yes. LTS support window is 6–12+ months depending on the branch. The idea is you’re not stuck forever, but you have a stable baseline long enough to plan upgrades.

[09:54] Elena Ruiz: And when a new LTS line comes out, do we have to jump immediately?

[09:59] Avery Johnson: No, there will be overlap. There’s usually an overlap period so you can migrate without rushing.

[10:07] Tom Sato: Can you clarify what “LTS reduces churn” means in numbers? Like fewer patches?

[10:12] Avery Johnson: It’s fewer unplanned upgrades. With mainline, you might feel pressure to upgrade to get a fix, then that introduces new behavior. With LTS, critical fixes are backported, so you stay within the same minor baseline. And release notes are slower-change: clearly categorized changes, known issues, upgrade notes. You get predictability.

[10:33] Priya Nair: That’s the main ask. Our current process is like… we get paged for a crash, then we chase upstream, then we upgrade, then we’re paged for a different thing.

[10:45] Bruno Silva: Right. The backport policy is designed to keep the diff small. If it’s a Sev1 crash fix, that can be cherry-picked into LTS without pulling in unrelated scheduler changes.

[10:57] Mark Feldman: But backports can be risky too. How do you prevent correctness issues?

[11:02] Bruno Silva: We require targeted tests and regression coverage. For LTS backports we don’t accept “drive-by refactors.” It’s minimal diff, strong tests, plus perf validation. And approvals require runtime lead + release manager, and sometimes SRE depending on severity.

[11:22] Rachel Kim: And from support: we’ll document known issues and workarounds rather than pushing experimental toggles.

[11:30] Elena Ruiz: Workarounds are fine if they’re documented.

[11:33] Avery Johnson: Let’s get concrete: Priya, what do you want to do for the pilot? Pin to a specific LTS patch and test rollback?

[11:41] Priya Nair: Yes. Ideally we want to run a drill: deploy new patch in staging, see metrics, then roll back. Also confirm that pinning prevents any surprise pull.

[11:54] Bruno Silva: Great. We can do that. On Helm, you’ll set something like:
- runtime.image.tag = 1.18.1-lts
- runtime.image.digest = sha256:… (optional but recommended)
And annotate with releaseNotesUrl. Then you can simulate a rollback with helm rollback.

[12:14] Tom Sato: Does the chart currently support both tag and digest?

[12:17] Bruno Silva: Yes, in the newer chart. If you’re on the older one, we’ll need to bump. I’ll send you the exact values snippet after this.

[12:28] Elena Ruiz: And the installer? We’re using Helm in staging but prod might use your installer.

[12:33] Bruno Silva: Installer supports pinning too. It writes a config file with the pinned version. If you want digest pinning, that’s supported in the latest build. We can provide a quick doc.

[12:47] Mark Feldman: Verification steps: do we get a public key? How do we verify checksums?

[12:53] Bruno Silva: We publish sha256 checksums. For signing, we’re moving to cosign for containers, but I don’t want to promise it’s fully GA today. For the pilot, checksums + provenance mapping to git tag is what we can guarantee.

[13:11] Mark Feldman: Okay, send whatever you have in writing.

[13:14] Avery Johnson: Will do. Also, we can set up a security follow-up focused on artifact verification.

[13:22] Priya Nair: Please.

[13:24] Rachel Kim: One more thing on rollbacks: you’ll want a validation checklist. For example: run a warmup load so caches are primed, compare p50/p95, check error logs for scheduler backpressure. We have a runbook we can share.

[13:42] Tom Sato: That’s helpful. We’d build that into our change ticket.

[13:46] Elena Ruiz: Can we also talk about whether LTS affects model availability? Like do we lose models or features.

[13:54] Avery Johnson: LTS isn’t a model catalog limitation per se, but it prioritizes stability over new runtime features. So if a brand-new optimization lands in mainline, it might not be backported. You still can run your models; you just might not get the newest scheduling tweak immediately.

[14:13] Priya Nair: That’s fine. We care more about predictability.

[14:17] Bruno Silva: Also important: compatibility matrix. Release notes will explicitly say what CUDA driver versions, GPU types, and Helm chart versions are compatible. That helps reduce “surprise” issues.

[14:33] Mark Feldman: Compatibility matrix is good. We had pain with driver mismatches.

[14:38] Tom Sato: Yeah, we had a node pool that was on the wrong NVIDIA driver and it caused weird kernel failures.

[14:44] Bruno Silva: Exactly the kind of thing we want to call out. Sometimes the transcription says “kernel,” but we mean GPU kernels.

[14:51] Elena Ruiz: (laughs) Yeah.

[14:54] Avery Johnson: Let’s check on the POC timeline. You’re aiming for an internal go/no-go by end of month, right?

[15:01] Priya Nair: Correct. We need to show: stable performance, pinned versions, rollback procedure, and security story is at least directionally acceptable.

[15:12] Mark Feldman: Plus audit trail. Like “what code is running.”

[15:16] Bruno Silva: That’s the provenance artifact. It ties the container to a git commit and build pipeline run ID.

[15:23] Mark Feldman: Okay.

[15:24] Avery Johnson: Elena, anything else from MLOps?

[15:28] Elena Ruiz: Just that the release notes need to be readable. Not like raw git logs. We need “what changed,” “what could break,” “known issues.”

[15:39] Rachel Kim: That’s exactly the LTS release notes format. It’s categorized, has known issues and mitigations, and upgrade notes.

[15:49] Priya Nair: Great.

[15:52] Tom Sato: One more rollback question: in a real incident, our RTO is like 15 minutes. Is that realistic?

[16:00] Bruno Silva: If the image is already present on nodes and you’re just rolling back the deployment, yes. If you have to pull images during the incident, network can slow it down. Best practice is pre-pull N and N-1 images on your node pools, or keep them warm.

[16:17] Tom Sato: Makes sense.

[16:19] Priya Nair: So we should keep two versions mirrored and pre-pulled.

[16:22] Bruno Silva: Exactly.

[16:24] Avery Johnson: Anything else on competitors? I know you mentioned Bedrock in the last call.

[16:29] Priya Nair: We evaluated Bedrock but data residency and VPC constraints are… complicated. That’s why Private matters.

[16:38] Elena Ruiz: And we tried Together’s dedicated, but we still want our own network controls.

[16:44] Avery Johnson: Understood.

[16:46] Mark Feldman: On the security side, we also looked at SageMaker endpoints but we’d still have to build a bunch of controls ourselves.

[16:54] Avery Johnson: Makes sense.

[16:56] Rachel Kim: From the CS side, the LTS program is basically to make Private feel enterprise-ready: predictable patching, better comms, and fewer emergency upgrades.

[17:09] Priya Nair: That’s the story we need internally.

[17:12] Avery Johnson: Cool. Let’s do a quick recap and then we can open it up for any last questions.

[17:18] Avery Johnson: Recap: You can pin versions in Helm and installer to an exact LTS patch, optionally pin by digest. Rollback is helm rollback or redeploying the previous pinned version. You should mirror and pre-pull N-1 images to hit RTO. We’ll share the exact Helm snippet, plus written verification steps and the pilot rollout/rollback checklist.

[17:43] Priya Nair: Sounds right.

[17:45] Mark Feldman: And schedule the security follow-up.

[17:48] Avery Johnson: Yes.

[17:50] Elena Ruiz: Can we also get a sample LTS release notes page? Even if it’s internal.

[17:55] Rachel Kim: Yes, we can provide an example format. It won’t be every detail, but you’ll see the structure.

[18:03] Tom Sato: And the canary suggestion: we’ll implement with Argo Rollouts.

[18:07] Bruno Silva: Great. I can also share recommended metrics to watch (p95, queue depth, error codes).

[18:15] Avery Johnson: Great. Any last questions?

[18:18] Priya Nair: No, this was helpful.

[18:20] Mark Feldman: Just send stuff in writing.

[18:22] Avery Johnson: Will do. Thanks all.

[18:26] (Transcript continues with light scheduling chatter; audio fades in/out)

[18:33] Avery Johnson: Okay, I’ll stop recording. Bye.
